story: In February 2023, astronomers discovered a city-bus-sized asteroid named 2023 DZ2 heading toward Earth. Measuring between 40 and 90 meters across, this space rock briefly carried odds of hitting our planet on March 27, 2026. However, additional tracking allowed scientists to completely rule out any impact threat, removing it from the Sentry Risk Table. On March 25, 2023, the asteroid made a dramatic close approach, passing safely between Earth and the Moon at a distance of roughly 175,000 kilometers—less than half the lunar distance. Traveling at over 17,000 miles per hour, its close proximity allowed amateur astronomers worldwide to spot the visitor using small telescopes and binoculars. Scientists used the flyby as a crucial planetary defense exercise, utilizing radar facilities like Goldstone to image the rapidly rotating, elongated object. Thanks to a resonance with Jupiter, Earth remains safe from 2023 DZ2 for the foreseeable future.
angle: A city-bus-sized asteroid was discovered just weeks before passing closer than the Moon, initially triggering impact worries for 2026 before scientists completely ruled out the threat.

claims.claim: Asteroid 2023 DZ2 is estimated to be between 40 and 90 meters in diameter.
The asteroid passed Earth on March 25, 2023.
It passed at a distance of approximately 175,000 kilometers, less than half the distance to the Moon.
The asteroid was briefly listed as a virtual impactor with a potential impact date in March 2026.
On March 21, 2023, the asteroid was removed from the Sentry Risk Table after further observations ruled out the 2026 impact.
The asteroid belongs to the Apollo group of near-Earth objects.
It was discovered using the Isaac Newton Telescope located at the Observatorio de Roque de los Muchachos on La Palma, Canary Islands, Spain.
The close approach allowed amateur astronomers and observers with small telescopes and binoculars to view the asteroid.
Its rotation period is about 6 minutes, suggesting an elongated shape.
The asteroid orbits the Sun approximately every 3.16 years.
